item.title: HEY NOW!
item.content:encoded:
The moment you've all been waiting for… announcing the winners of the SCP-3000 contest!

THE GRAND PRIZE

Congratulations to ARD, Joreth and Kaktus for their success in writing SCP-3000: Anantashesha!

The Winner's Circle

Congratulations to The Top Five!

SCP-3001 - Red Reality by OZ Ouroboros!

SCP-3333 - Tower by Jekeled!

SCP-3002 - Attempts to Assassinate Thought by tretter!

SCP-3003 - The End of History by Communism Will Win!

SCP-3999 - I Am At The Centre Of Everything That Happens To Me by LordStonefish!

Some contest context, and cause for thought. In the 1000 contest, the top three entries were rated at +46, +39 and +27 with fifteen total entries. In the 2000 contest the top three rated +189, +166, +147 with a total of 30 entries. The SCP-3000 contest has blown that turnout out of the water in a big way. Here we have all of our top six entries being +200. That's incredible. This was also done in a much more crowded field with 42 entries in the positives at the end of contention. That's more than both of our previous x000 contests combined. It's not quite that much, 45 is more than 42, but we still had all our top 20 articles be +100. Well done guys.

For our amazing contestants who did not make it into the Winner's Circle you may rename(via the options menu at the bottom of the page) and move your entry to a desired slot as soon as now! Be sure to check the discussion here to see which spots people have requested holds on. Once you have moved your SCP into the spot you want, sit tight and a staff member will be along to edit the article name into the Series IV list, as it is currently locked.

Congratulations to the winners and the contestants. Thanks for reading everybody!

item.title: Wherein I attempt to Review the Contest
item.content:encoded:
By my count, there are 41 positively rated entries that will be moving to Series IV slots tomorrow, three negatively rated entries that will not, 16 that were deleted during the posting period by the deletions process, and two that were self-deleted and not reposted; for a total of 62 contest entries. Did I miss any?

I have read and voted (or chosen to not vote) on all currently extant entries, I have commented on most of them as well. I apologize if I missed some of the deleted ones before they were gone.

Overall there's a lot of really excellent material here, and some really good horror writing specifically.

Rather than attempt to address each article individually, I'll just list my top five favorites:

+ show block
– hide block
  1. The More You Know by psul: This takes creepy real world behavior in the form of sexual manipulation, mixes it with cosmic horror and uses it in a tight narrative with believable, sympathetic characters. Cooper is exactly the kind of horror protagonist I love: smart, competent, brave, and certainly doomed anyway. The excerpts from The More You Know capture the same sense of alien wrong-ness that the Star Signals excerpts have in SCP-1425, another favorite of mine. I think of all the entries, this was the most effective for me as a horror story.
  2. Falling Out by WrongJohnSilver: It takes a neat trick to turn dense scientifically plausible technical writing into a tense edge-of-your seat monster yarn, and this does it. It also does one of my favorite things in horror fiction by making me afraid of a seemingly harmless everyday phenomenon: hypnic jerks.
  3. Red Reality by OZ Ouroboros: A much more personal take on the fear of solitude than my own entry. Scranton is a very believable and worthy narrator for this journey. The use of the imagery of the blinking red light being the only visible thing in this universe and the anchor around which Scranton retains his identity is a lovely and effective one. This article handily overcomes my usually resistance to the reality physics technobabble of Humes and SRAs by using them for something other than a convenient narrative handwave but rather as central elements of the story.
  4. Attempts to Assassinate Thought by tretter: This is a very personal horror, of identity loss and false memory, cast into an epic, apocalyptic scale. It's also a great revenge story. I really like the Wagnerian touch of having the Foundation's own measures to avert doom in the Lethe program reverberate into the thing that dooms them. The dwindling O5 is a brilliant touch as well. This article also seamlessly uses the ListPages module to tell a story through iterative documents.
  5. The Light that Died by Silberescher: Masterful and highly plausible use of incomplete information. The tantalizing questions as to exactly what the relationship between the pink light and the testing booth is are delightfully unanswered. The corruption of the researcher by the anti-thought of Fifthism is pure Lovecraftian cosmic horror. I did find the tone and style of the researcher's comments to read very much like the kind of thing that horror videogame writers like to have the narrator declaim during loading screens — which I think works well once the researcher is far gone but is jarring in the earlier entries — but this is really a minor stylistic quibble.

Overall, only two of these are in the actual top five entries in the contest although all five are very respectively rated, so I suppose my tastes aren't too far off of the general wiki's.

Some observations about trends, themes, and highlights from the contest:

+ show block
– hide block
  • There are several entries that primarily developed a narrative through exploration logs: Anantashesha, The Tower, The More You Know, Chronos, Bone Orchard, To Force the Hand of God, The Reliquary, Hoffman's Nightmare, and Alternative Facts.
  • Three entries had a dwindling Foundation in an apocalyptic scenario: Attempts to Assassinate Thought, my own Peaceful Sunday, and the now author-deleted "When Day Breaks".
  • Three entries involved hynogogic sleep phenomena: Sleep Paralysis, Falling Out, and Hoffman's Nightmare.
  • Four entries felt deeply personal: I am at the Center of Everything that Happens to Me, Depression, Abdominal Pain and The Love of Fools.
  • Over half the entries had a monster or monsters.
  • Several entries had a degraded or compromised reality as a primary horrific element, among them: Red Reality, Chronos, Alternative Facts, I am at the Center of Everything that Happens to Me, Best Intentions and Chessland.
  • Two entries both involved extradimensional spaces and red colored lights!
  • While many entries aimed at a grand epic scale, several were more modest horror tales. Notably there was a solid straightforward ghost story, Rachel Parks, a witch legend, The Wicker With Lives!, a monster from folklore, The Orcadian Horseman, and a old-school creepypasta-ish unique monster, The Nursery.
  • Three entries involved weird video: Parousia, Twice the Number One and Hideous Mountain.
  • Four entries had arthropods or athropodoids (and therefore entomophobia or arachnophobia) as primary elements: The End of History, Falling Out, Imago, and A Fly.
  • Suprisingly few entries involved GOIs: The More You Know, Peaceful Sunday, and The Light that Died all involved the Fifth Church, Bone Orchard involved the Sarkic Cults, Sleep Paralysis involved the Oneiroi Collective, ...And We'd Rather Remain in the Darkness had the Church of the Broken God, and The Bones of What You Believe introduced two new related GOIs — The Verdant and The Veldt.
  • Four entries used ListPages modules: Self-Insert, Depression, Attempts to Assassinate Thought and author-deleted "The Hum". This nearly doubles the SCP articles that use this module, so it might represent a new trend.

Some otherwise notable entries:

  • Chessland was partially written by Markov chain and had some really well-crafted Umberto Ecco-esque prose buried after a lot of nonsensical stuff that most readers seem to have run out of patience with. I really hope the author tries to rewrite this in a more digestible form.
  • Parousia isn't an SCP, which makes it seem, to me, as inappropriate for SCP-3000. Otherwise I really liked it.
  • World of Two Artists is developed around some beautifully haunting paintings by the author.

I think that Series IV is definitely off to a solid, high-quality start!

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Falling Out has spiders, disease, prions, sleep disturbances, and a realization that all these things have been living with us for millennia, and we have always been prey. It even has a jumpscare.

The science serves to demonstrate how all this could actually be true.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
If you mean "there are no lazy one-note straight plays of generic fears", that kind of goes without saying.

A lot of entries do interesting things with common and semi-common fears, though: The aforementioned Sleep Paralysis mixes the fears of vulnerability while sleeping and the fear of having your irrational fears realized, Falling Out combines arachnophobia with a dash of cosmic horror, Abdominal Pain is classic body horror crossed with medical horror. Causal-Absent Paranoia is like a greatest hits of common and semi-common phobias- darkness, mirrors, being hunted, agoraphobia, isolation, claustrophobia, simple paranoia…
